Here's a complete breakdown of everything in the guide — let me walk you through what's there and add a few extra nuances that are worth knowing explicitly.

The core idea — why Anki works at all

About 50% of new information is forgotten within an hour without review, 70% within 24 hours, and 90% within a week. But each time you successfully recall and review an item, the forgetting curve flattens — it decays more slowly because retrieval has strengthened the memory trace. Anki schedules each card to appear just before you'd forget it, and a 2025 study published in the International Journal of Asian Social Science Research confirms that active retrieval practice — trying to remember the answer — is significantly more effective than passive review, like rereading.

The four self-rating buttons — what they actually do

When you flip a card, you press Again / Hard / Good / Easy. Again is for words you can't remember at all. Hard is for words that take several minutes of concentration. Good is for words you recall without much effort, perhaps within five to fifteen seconds. Easy is for words you recall instantly. Anki uses this rating combined with an "ease factor" to calculate when the card shows next. The formula is roughly: next interval = last interval × ease. Cards you consistently get right drift toward longer, more stable intervals. Cards you keep missing stay on short cycles until they stick.

The four main workflows

The biggest mistake new learners make is creating "word-to-word" cards (Apple = Manzana). These are fragile because they lack context. Instead, use sentence mining — taking a sentence from a book, movie, or podcast and turning it into a card.

The pre-made deck approach is for beginners. The Japanese Core 2000 Step 01 deck is probably the most popular beginner vocab deck — it pairs basic words with audio and images, and by the time you finish Core 6000, you'll have a solid foundation for reading native material.

Sentence mining is for intermediate and advanced learners. Sentence mining combines several things that make vocabulary stick: context (words learned in real sentences), personal relevance (words come from content you chose and enjoy), the IKEA effect (cards you make yourself are easier to learn), multi-channel reinforcement (cards often include audio, images, and text from the original scene), and spaced repetition.

The immersion method (Refold/AJATT) takes it furthest. In this approach, the role of the SRS is to help you understand more of your immersion, not to help you produce the language yourself. Therefore, all cards are comprehension cards, not production cards. The front of a card can feature either an audio recording or written text — never both at the same time, since you wouldn't truly be testing either listening or reading ability.

The critical settings mistake almost everyone makes

You must configure the software to prevent "review hell," where you wake up to hundreds of overdue cards. Adjusting the "New Cards per Day" limit is the most important step for beginners. Setting this to 10 or 20 prevents an exponential explosion of reviews in the second and third weeks of study. The rule is simple: reviews first, new cards second. If you are short on time, skip the new cards for the day, but never skip your reviews.

The leeches problem

Some cards you'll fail over and over. Don't mine words that are extremely niche or unlikely to appear again, or words you already sort of know. Mining too many cards is easy — you can save 30+ cards in a session, but if you can't review them all, they pile up. Delete cards that aren't useful rather than letting them create a backlog.

The most important principle of all

Anki is a supplement, not a replacement for immersion. The goal of Anki is to make you recognize words in the wild. If you spend two hours on Anki and zero hours listening to the language, you are training your brain to be an expert at flashcards rather than an expert at speaking. What Anki does well is help you memorize discrete pieces of information — vocabulary, kanji, verb conjugations, grammar patterns. What Anki could never do alone is make you fluent or teach you to understand native content comfortably.

The interactive guide above lets you click through every card type and workflow with real examples. The most useful things to explore are the "What people learn" section (click each category for a real card example) and the "Good vs. bad card" toggle, which makes the design principles concrete.

The video adds a few genuinely useful things not covered before — let me pull those out first, then build the full step-by-step walkthrough you're asking for.

What the video adds that's new:

The creator makes a strong point that the goal of Anki is not to "know" a word perfectly after learning it in the app — it's just to get a rough recognition so that when you encounter the word in real content, your brain can hook onto it and gradually build the true understanding through context. He uses the Japanese word 気 (ki) as an example — the dictionary definition is "spirit, mind, heart, nature, disposition, intention, will, motivation, mood, feeling" — and points out that no flashcard can teach you what that word actually feels like in use. Only hours of hearing it in natural sentences can do that. Anki just makes sure you recognize it when it shows up.

He also recommends using only Again and Good — not Hard or Easy — because Hard and Easy cause big deviations in the scheduling algorithm that mess up your intervals over time. Most online guides don't say this clearly.

He also explains that missing days is totally fine — just don't add new cards until you've cleared the backlog. Don't quit because of a pile-up.

[Interactive Widget: anki_day_by_day_user_journey]

Let me now answer the specific questions you asked, because a few things deserve extra clarity beyond what the interactive walkthrough shows.

"Does he just see the German word or the English word first?"

It depends on the deck — this is a real choice. Most good German vocabulary decks show the German word on the front and English on the back. This trains recognition: you see German → you recall English meaning. That's the most useful skill for understanding German content (reading, listening). Some learners flip it — English on front, German on back — to train production (speaking, writing). The video creator specifically says Anki is mainly for comprehension, not production, so German → English is the standard approach.

"What happens on Day 1 when he sees a word for the very first time — isn't it impossible to know it?"

Yes — and that's totally fine. On Day 1, seeing "das Haus" for the first time, you just look at the front, think for a second (even if you have no idea), then press "Show answer" to see the back. You read the back — "the house", example sentence, audio. You now press Good. You're not being tested yet; you're being introduced. The testing comes tomorrow when it reappears and you try to recall it from memory without the back being visible.

"On Day 15, what happens first — does it ask him some words and ask him to say the answer?"

Yes. Day 15 opens with your review queue — Anki shows you the front of a card (German word only, no meaning shown), and you try to recall the answer silently in your head. Then you press "Show answer" to see the back and check yourself. Then you press Again or Good based on whether you actually knew it. Anki doesn't check your answer for you — you self-grade honestly. The whole system runs on your own honesty about whether you really knew it.

On image occlusion specifically — the key thing to understand is that it's not a separate type of learning. It's just a way of making a specific kind of card where the "question" is a visual with something hidden, and the "answer" is revealing what was hidden. People use it most for things that have a natural visual structure: body parts on a diagram, room objects in a picture, countries on a map, labels on a food diagram. For language learning specifically it's fantastic for concrete nouns — things you can point at — because the spatial context of the image becomes part of the memory.

To pull together the most important points and back them with the specific research:

There is real scientific value — but it's concentrated in one half of your idea.

The "new word → comprehensible video" half is strongly supported. In a direct comparison, multimedia instruction led to significantly higher vocabulary gains on the immediate test compared to text-only instruction, and multimedia learning also promoted greater long-term retention. The effect sizes are large: the percentages of correct answers for words with video and text, picture and text, and text alone were 87%, 67%, and 53% respectively. And the mechanism is well understood — the picture superiority effect is a dual coding phenomenon where people have better memory of pictures over words; when we encounter a word it is encoded verbally so there is only a single path for retrieval, whereas a picture is encoded through both visual and verbal pathways, so the memory trace is stronger. One detail that should matter to you specifically: multimedia was found particularly beneficial for learners with lower verbal working memory capacity — so the video helps your strugglers most, which are exactly the learners who otherwise quit.

The "review → video" half is where you must be careful. The danger is that you accidentally replace Anki's core mechanism. Research demonstrates that retrieval practice is a powerful mnemonic enhancer, often producing large gains in long-term retention relative to repeated studying — things are impressed better by active than by passive repetition. Karpicke and Blunt (2011) showed active retrieval improved retention by 50% compared to passive review, while passive study methods like re-reading often lead to an overestimation of one's understanding. If your review video just shows the words with meanings, that's passive re-exposure — it would weaken the system you're trying to improve.

The fix is simple and it's the heart of my recommendation: keep recall first, always. The learner tries to retrieve each word from memory (normal Anki), grades themselves, and then gets the comprehensible video as feedback. This doesn't fight the testing effect — it strengthens it, because retrieval practice is often effective even without feedback, but feedback enhances the benefits of testing. Your video is rich, contextual feedback.

On your batch-story idea specifically — it's genuinely good, but reframe it. Don't let the story video be the review. Do the 10 individual recall cards first, then play the story that weaves all 10 words together as an end-of-session immersion reward. That way you preserve retrieval, add a narrative-context encoding boost, and — maybe most valuably — you make finishing reviews enjoyable, which directly attacks Anki's biggest failure mode (people quitting from boredom). That motivational lever is probably your largest real-world impact even though it's the hardest to measure.

One honest caveat on the evidence: there is some nuance for review specifically. One study of dual-subtitled videos found that viewing with repetition produced greater vocabulary gains than no repetition, with evidence indicating the superiority of immediate repetitions over spaced repetitions. But that measured re-watching, not active recall — your "spaced retrieval + video-as-feedback" design sidesteps the tension entirely.

For your actual learning project, build the smallest safe version: German A1, vocab cards only, video on new-word introduction, recall-first on review with video as the answer. It reuses your entire existing five-stage pipeline, it's scientifically the strongest part of the idea, and it risks nothing. [Interactive Widget: anki_ai_automation_competitive_landscape]

To summarize the most important findings in plain terms, with the evidence:

The image and audio parts of your idea are completely solved already. Auto-attaching images to flashcards is everywhere — one developer's tool generates an image prompt then sends it to your chosen image provider, and handles SSML parsing, pause timing, and audio normalization automatically, even supporting voice cloning. Migaku, the dominant immersion tool, creates media-rich flashcards that include your word, its definition, the sentence it appears in, a translation, a screenshot of your show, and a snippet of the show's audio. So "image + audio per word" is not novel — it's table stakes.

Your "story video weaving the review words" idea has been built — but only as text and audio, not video. This is the most important finding, and it strongly validates your instinct. Langua does exactly this: you choose words from your flashcard deck that you've saved from conversations or immersion content and weave them into AI-generated mini stories, which is a fun and creative way to learn new vocab since seeing vocab in different contexts is key. Lenguia goes even further with a dedicated engine — it uses a context-based spaced repetition system that creates tailor-made stories, where your flashcards and other new words you should review automatically get placed inside the stories, using 83 narrative structures and 25 tones. Two separate teams independently converged on your exact pedagogical idea. That's about as strong a validation signal as you can get — but notice they both stopped at text + audio.

The actual video-generation version appears unoccupied. The tools that involve video all use existing footage — Migaku and Wordy mine clips and screenshots from real shows and Netflix. None generate new video as the flashcard medium. This is genuine white space.

But the reason it's empty is both a feature and a warning. It's white space partly because the video models only became good enough in 2025–2026 — which is precisely the constraint your own strategy document identified as having just lifted. But it's also empty because, as your own cost analysis flagged, video is expensive ($1.50+ per clip versus fractions of a cent for text). The text-story approach exists because it's nearly free. So the gap is real, the timing is genuinely right, and the pedagogy is validated — but the unit economics are the thing standing between you and everyone else.

For a learning/course project rather than a scaled business, that's an ideal position: you're building something that genuinely doesn't exist yet, on top of pedagogy two funded competitors have already proven works, and you only have to build one novel layer — your existing Comprehensible Engine video pipeline plugged into the well-established AnkiConnect plumbing that every other tool already uses.

Looking at your screenshots, the ~400 German decks actually cluster into about 8 distinct types, and only some are suitable for your video pipeline. Let me lay them all out.

[Interactive Widget: german_anki_deck_types_for_video_pipeline]

The eight types are laid out above with real examples from your own screenshots. Here's the reasoning that matters for your decision, pulling the threads together.

The thing to internalize is that the deck's structure matters far more than its language level for your purpose. A "German A1 deck" could be a picturable-word deck, a sentence deck, a grammar drill, or a dictionary dump — and those four demand completely different things from your video pipeline. So the right mental model isn't "which A1 deck is best," it's "which type produces words my pipeline can actually turn into comprehensible-input video."

When you sort by that question, five of the eight types drop away immediately. Grammar decks, pronunciation decks, and dictionary dumps fail because their content isn't meaning-in-a-scene at all — you can't film "the dative case" or a minimal-pair sound contrast. Pure frequency lists fail for a subtler reason: they're excellent for real learning but they front-load exactly the un-filmable words (der, und, aber, sein), because those are the most frequent words in the language. And full official wordlists (like the Goethe A1 926-card deck) fail softly — they're clean and well-made, but they faithfully mix concrete words like Apfel right next to abstract ones like Vorsicht (caution) and kulturell (cultural), so you'd have to filter them yourself.

That leaves three viable types, and they're not competitors so much as three rungs of ambition. The thematic food deck is the safest possible first test because a single topic is inherently concrete and gives you one coherent story world. The Fluent Forever 625 is the best true foundation deck because the hard filtering work — removing every non-visual word — was literally the design principle behind that list. And the sentence-based decks like Languages on Fire are the most comprehensible-input-native, because a sentence already hands you the scene to animate rather than making you invent context around a lone word.

My honest read: start on the food deck to prove the pipeline end-to-end on something where nothing can go wrong, then move to the Fluent Forever 625 as your real foundation. That sequencing lets you validate the hardest technical part (generating a good CI clip and weaving a story) on a set where every single word is guaranteed filmable, before you scale to the broader vocabulary.

One question that will sharpen the choice: do you picture your pipeline generating video from single words (where 625 or the food deck fit best) or from whole sentences (where Languages on Fire fits best)? That one decision determines which of the three is your actual starting point — want to think that through together?
